name: Gymnastic rings
lead: Gymnastic rings are a pair of rings suspended from a frame by straps, used both as an artistic gymnastics apparatus and as a bodyweight training tool. In competition the still rings event is traditionally performed only by male gymnasts because of its demand for upper-body strength [1]. In calisthenics, rings can be used for dips, front and back levers and muscle-ups [2].
In looksmaxxing, rings are mentioned as a way to build the upper body physique associated with gymnasts. No trials were found that test rings against other training tools for appearance outcomes.

paras: Under the International Gymnastics Federation norms described by Wikipedia, competition rings have an 18 cm inner diameter and a 2.8 cm profile diameter, hang from straps and steel cables 300 cm from a rigid frame, and are set 50 cm apart at their attachment points [1]. Gymnasts usually wear grips [1].

Routines combine swings, strength holds and a dismount, with skills such as the iron cross, in which the arms are held out to the sides [1]. Judges deduct for bent arms and for leaning on the straps or cables [1].

Rings appear in bodyweight programs for exercises such as dips, front and back levers and muscle-ups [2]. A 2017 study cited by Wikipedia described calisthenics generally as an effective way to improve posture, strength and body composition, while Wikipedia flags hypertrophy claims as lacking citation [2]. That evidence concerns calisthenics broadly rather than rings specifically.
No studies found on rings as a training tool for physique outcomes.

card.summary: Suspended rings for bodyweight training; the gymnast physique is the draw, but no studies compare them for looks.
card.note: Training-specific evidence is lacking; calisthenics research is general.

quick.overview:
Gymnastic rings are straps with rings you hang from a frame or bar to do dips, levers and muscle-ups. They are the apparatus behind gymnasts' upper-body strength.

Research on calisthenics in general is mildly positive for strength and body composition, but rings themselves have not been compared with other tools for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Because the rings move freely, bodyweight exercises on them require extra stabilization from the shoulders and arms.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to rings were found in the sources reviewed. Advanced skills such as the iron cross are demanding strength elements in competition.
